title: Commission strengthens Europe’s position as the world’s leading tourism destination
source_name: 欧盟委员会交通与运输总司
content: The European Commission today presented a new EU Sustainable Tourism Strategy, to increase the sector’s competitiveness, sustainability and resilience. The strategy will help businesses grow and workers build skills; it will support destinations in developing a balanced tourism offer; improve travellers’ experiences and maintain Europe as the world’s leading tourism destination. Tourism is a key part of Europe’s economy. It contributes to 10% of the EU’s Gross Value Added, supports more than 20 million jobs and includes 5 million businesses, of which 99% are small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). While tourism supports local economies across the EU, it also cultivates culture and shapes Europe’s global influence. At the same time, in the current global context, the tourism sector faces several challenges, including geopolitical uncertainty, skills and talent shortages, the impacts of climate change and changing traveller expectations. Europe’s tourism sector has already proven resilient, and Europeans’ appetite for travel remains strong, with 76% planning a trip in the next six months. Shared challenges require a shared approach. The strategy will therefore help tourism businesses, especially SMEs, and destination management organisations access skills, digital tools and data to innovate and grow sustainably. It will also look for ways to reduce unnecessary administrative barriers. Flagship actions include the EU Tourism Academy, the EU Tourism Observatory, the Common European Tourism Data Space, the EU simplification initiative on tourism and continued work towards a seamless European travel area. The strategy will promote tourism that benefits visitors, businesses and local communities. The Commission will support destinations to better manage visitor flows, encourage travel throughout the year and improve preparedness for potential crises. Actions include an EU Model for Tourism Management, a Council recommendation, a Toolbox for Balanced Tourism and an EU Tourism Crisis Coordination Network. Europe accounts for around 40% of international tourist arrivals worldwide, making it the world’s lead destination. The strategy will further boost Europe’s global appeal through stronger international cooperation. This includes cooperation with international organisations, such as UN Tourism and the OECD, tourism dialogues with key partner countries and regions, and promotion of Europe through the Destination Europe framework. To amplify the visibility of European destinations and its hidden gems, there will also be new European Capitals of Tourism Awards. To deliver the strategy, a new EU Tourism Alliance will bring together national, regional and local authorities, tourism businesses and stakeholders. The Commission will continue supporting tourism-related actions through relevant EU programmes and funding instruments. Background Tourism is one of Europe’s most important economic and social sectors. This new EU strategy for tourism delivers on the Commission’s 2026 Work Programme commitment to strengthen the sector’s competitiveness and resilience, as well as on President von der Leyen’s mission letter to Commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas. The mission letter tasked the Commissioner to intensify the EU’s efforts to promote a resilient and competitive tourism sector, in line with the EU Agenda for Tourism 2030. title: Air Plan Approval; District of Columbia; Enhanced Vehicle Emission Inspection and Maintenance (I/M) Program Revision and Basic I/M Program Certification for Moderate Nonattainment Areas Under the 2015 Ozone NAAQS
content: ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY 40 CFR Part 52 [EPA-R03-OAR-2026-1024; FRL-12072-01-R3] Air Plan Approval; District of Columbia; Enhanced Vehicle Emission Inspection and Maintenance (I/M) Program Revision and Basic I/M Program Certification for Moderate Nonattainment Areas Under the 2015 Ozone NAAQS AGENCY: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). ACTION: Proposed rule. SUMMARY: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing to approve a State Implementation Plan (SIP) revision submitted by the District of Columbia (DC, or the District). This revision incorporates regulatory updates made to the District's Enhanced motor vehicle emissions inspection and maintenance (I/M) program since the EPA's last SIP approval. The SIP revision also serves to certify that the District's existing Enhanced I/M program meets Clean Air Act (CAA) requirements for a Basic I/M program for the District's portion of the Washington, DC-MD-VA nonattainment area (the Washington nonattainment area) for the 2015 Ozone National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS). DATES: Written comments must be received on or before December 7, 2026. ADDRESSES: Submit your comments, identified by Docket ID No. EPA-R03-OAR-2025-0304 at www.regulations.gov, or via email to gordon.mike@epa.gov. For comments submitted at Regulations.gov, follow the online instructions for submitting comments. Once submitted, comments cannot be edited or removed from Regulations.gov . For either manner of submission, EPA may publish any comment received to its public docket. Do not submit electronically any information you consider to be confidential business information (CBI) or other information whose disclosure is restricted by statute. Multimedia submissions (audio, video, etc.) must be accompanied by a written comment. The written comment is considered the official comment and should include discussion of all points you wish to make. EPA will generally not consider comments or comment contents located outside of the primary submission ( i.e., on the web, cloud, or other file sharing system). Background On June 7, 2024, the District of Columbia Department of Energy and Environment (DOEE) submitted a revision to its SIP to incorporate administrative and regulatory and statutory authority updates to the District's Enhanced I/M program made since the program's prior approval into the DC SIP in 1999. The June 2024 SIP revision also demonstrates through an emissions modeling analysis that the DC I/M program meets applicable CAA requirements for both Basic and Enhanced I/M programs for the District portion of the Washington, DC-MD-VA ozone nonattainment area (also referred to as the Washington area). A. Overview of EPA's Proposed Action On June 7, 2024, the District of Columbia submitted a SIP revision to both update its I/M program SIP to incorporate the most current iteration of DC I/M program regulations and to demonstrate that the program continues to meet applicable CAA requirements for an Enhanced I/M program. Further, the District's June 2024 SIP revision intends to satisfy the Basic I/M program requirement for Moderate nonattainment areas under the 2015 ozone NAAQS. In October 2022, the Washington nonattainment area was reclassified to Moderate, upon failure to attain the 2015 ozone NAAQS by the area's August 2021 Marginal area attainment date. Because the District had an existing Enhanced I/M program, the Basic I/M SIP requirement can be met by demonstrating that the District's existing Enhanced I/M program meets all applicable CAA Basic I/M requirements, including the requirement for a modeling analysis to demonstrate that the Washington Moderate ozone nonattainment area's I/M program meets or exceeds the emission reduction levels of the corresponding Basic I/M performance standard. The EPA is proposing to approve the District's revised I/M program as being consistent with the applicable CAA Basic and Enhanced I/M requirements under CAA sections 182 and 184, and with the EPA's I/M requirements. 1 The EPA is proposing to approve both updates made to the District's existing, SIP-approved I/M program as well as its certification that the existing program meets CAA Basic I/M requirements. 1 See 40 CFR part 51, subpart S. B. 2015 Ozone NAAQS Background and EPA Designation of the Washington Area On October 1, 2015, the EPA revised the primary and secondary NAAQS for ozone to a level of 0.70 parts per million (ppm) (based on the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average concentration, averaged over three years) to provide increased protection of human health and the environment. 2 The 2015 ozone NAAQS retains the same general form and averaging time as the 0.75 ppm NAAQS set in 2008, but is set at a more protective level. On June 4, 2018 (effective August 3, 2018), the EPA designated the Washington, DC-MD-VA area (including the District of Columbia) as Marginal nonattainment for the 2015 ozone NAAQS. 3 Areas designated as Marginal nonattainment were required to attain the 2015 ozone NAAQS by no later than August 3, 2021 (three years from the effective date of designation). 2 See 80 FR 65292 (Oct. 26, 2015). 3 See 83 FR 25795 (June 4, 2018), codified at 40 CFR 81.309. On October 7, 2022, the EPA determined that the Washington nonattainment area failed to attain the 2015 ozone NAAQS by its August 3, 2021 Marginal area attainment date and reclassified the area by operation of law from Marginal to Moderate nonattainment. 4 Moderate areas were required to attain the 2015 ozone NAAQS by no later than six years after the effective date of initial designation, or August 3, 2024. As a result of this reclassification, the Washington area became subject to Moderate area requirements under CAA section 182(b), under CAA statutory implementation timeframes, which were reiterated in the EPA's October 7, 2022 reclassification rule. 4 See 87 FR 60897 (Oct. 7, 2022). With the reclassification to Moderate, the Washington nonattainment area is required to submit a Basic I/M SIP. The State can meet these Basic I/M requirements through certification that their existing, SIP-approved I/M program meets Basic I/M requirements for the 2015 ozone NAAQS. C. Clean Air Act Requirements for I/M Programs The CAA mandates I/M for certain urbanized ozone and carbon monoxide (CO) nonattainment areas based upon certain criteria, such as air quality status, population, and/or geographic location. I/M is the periodic inspection of the emissions control systems of motor vehicles. CAA section 182 requires I/M programs in areas of States most impacted by ground-level ozone pollution (to varying levels of I/M program stringency, either Basic or Enhanced) dependent upon the severity of an area's air pollution and its population. States with nonattainment areas classified by the EPA as Moderate that exceed CAA-established population thresholds are required to implement a CAA-defined, Basic I/M program. Areas classified as Serious or worse ozone nonattainment that exceed CAA-established, population thresholds must enact an Enhanced I/M program. Areas that fail to attain the ozone NAAQS by the CAA deadline for doing so are reclassified to a higher nonattainment classification, and as such may be newly subject to I/M requirements, or to re-evaluate and (if necessary) to upgrade an existing I/M program to a more stringent I/M program type. Moderate and Enhanced nonattainment I/M requirements are set forth at CAA section 182(b)(4) and section 182(c)(3), respectively. Pursuant to CAA section 182(b)(4), States with ozone nonattainment areas classified as Moderate are required to implement a Basic I/M program in certain applicable areas. The Federal rule addressing I/M program requirements are provided at 40 CFR part 51, subpart S. CAA section 184 further requires implementation of Enhanced I/M programs in metropolitan areas of an ozone transport region (OTR) and established an OTR for an area that geographically extends from the Washington, DC area northward to Maine. OTR I/M requirements apply regardless of ozone nonattainment classification, based solely on metropolitan area size and population. 5 Within the OTR, geographic scope is established to be any metropolitan statistical area (MSA), or portion thereof, with a 1990 population of 100,000 or more, as defined by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB). 6 5 See CAA 184(b)(1)(a). 6 See CAA section 184(b)(1)(A) and 40 CFR 51.350(a)(1). D. DC's Prior, Approved Enhanced I/M Program SIP With enactment of the 1990 CAA, the EPA classified the Washington, DC-MD-VA area by operation of law in 1991 as Serious nonattainment for the 1979 1-hour ozone NAAQS, 7 triggering the Serious CAA ozone nonattainment area requirement to establish an Enhanced I/M program in urbanized portion of the Washington ozone nonattainment area having a 1980 population over 200,000 persons. 8 Since the Washington area also lies in the CAA-established OTR, Enhanced I/M is also required under the CAA section 184 OTR Enhanced I/M requirement, applicable to the MSA having a 1990 population of 100,000 or more. 9 7 The EPA designated the Washington, DC-MD-VA area as nonattainment for ozone for the 1979 1-hour ozone NAAQS, with the area classified as Serious ozone nonattainment (56 FR 56694, Nov. 6, 1991). 8 CAA section 182(c)(3)(A) and 40 CFR 51.350(a)(1). 9 CAA section 184(b)(1)(A) and 40 CFR 51.350(a)(2). The EPA approved the District of Columbia's Enhanced I/M SIP in a final rule, 10 which converted to full approval the EPA's conditional approval of the DC I/M program. 11 The District began officially testing vehicles under its SIP-approved Enhanced I/M program in April 1999. 10 See 64 FR 31498, June 11, 1999. 11 See 63 FR 29955, June 2, 1998. II. Summary of the District of Columbia's June 7, 2024 SIP Submittal On June 7, 2024, the District of Columbia submitted a SIP revision amending its I/M program approved by the EPA to the DC SIP in 1999. The June 2024 SIP revision serves to incorporate by reference I/M program regulations codified under DC. Municipal Regulations (DCMR) Title 18, Chapters 6 and 7, as amended by a change in legal authority for the program (the District's “Vehicle Inspection Improvement Amendment Act of 2009”) that enacted many of the DCMR regulatory revisions that comprise this SIP revision. Also part of the District's June 2024 SIP revision is a Basic I/M Certification SIP demonstrating that the revised DC I/M program meets applicable CAA requirements for a Basic I/M program required for a Moderate ozone nonattainment area. This I/M certification SIP is comprised of a performance standard modeling (PSM) demonstration showing that the enacted DC I/M program meets the CAA Basic I/M performance standard, as well as showing that the SIP meets all other requirements for a Basic I/M program. A Basic I/M SIP is required for the District's portion of the Washington, DC-MD-VA 2015 ozone nonattainment area, as a result of the area having been reclassified by EPA in 2022 from Marginal to Moderate. 12 12 See “Determinations of Attainment by the Attainment Date, Extensions of the Attainment Date, and Reclassification of Areas Classified as Marginal for the 2015 Ozone National Ambient Air Quality Standards” (87 FR 60897, Oct. 7, 2022). The EPA's review of the elements of the District's June 7, 2024 I/M SIP revision (as well as our analysis of these SIP revisions for compliance with the CAA and EPA's I/M Rule 13 ) is described in detail below. 13 See CAA sections 182 and 184 for applicable I/M requirements, as well as EPA's I/M requirements rule, at 40 CFR 51.350 through 51.373. Amendment of the existing, approved SIP to revise a CAA-required control measure requires that the state demonstrate that the revised measure continues to meet applicable CAA requirements. In the case of the Enhanced I/M program, this requires that the revised program meets all Enhanced requirements set forth at CAA 182(c)(3) and at the EPA's I/M rule, including an I/M PSM analysis showing that that the program meets the Enhanced I/M performance standard. However, DC's revision to the SIP-approved I/M program consist entirely of regulatory updates and other non-regulatory updates to the program that are administrative in nature that do not change program applicability, the inspection process, or any other aspect of the program that can be shown to change the emissions benefits of the prior, SIP-approved program. Given the administrative and clerical nature of the DC regulatory updates, the EPA has determined that an Enhanced I/M PSM analysis is not necessary for this action. The EPA's review of the regulatory updates to the program was summarized in this action, with further detail on our review provided in the accompanying technical support document (TSD) for this action. C. I/M Performance Standard Modeling (PSM) Demonstration To Demonstrate Compliance With CAA Requirements for a Basic I/M Program Applicable to Moderate Ozone Nonattainment Areas The CAA and I/M regulations allow States a great deal of flexibility in designing their I/M programs as long as the applicable I/M performance standard is met. An I/M performance standard is a collection of program design elements, to which a state's I/M program is compared in terms of its potential to reduce emissions of the ozone precursors. A PSM analysis is performed using the most recent version of the EPA's Motor Vehicle Emissions Simulator Model (MOVES) available at the time of analysis. The PSM demonstration compares the resultant MOVES-derived emissions levels, expressed as a comparison of tons per day of the ozone precursors NO X and VOCs from onroad mobile sources in the I/M area. The EPA's I/M rule sets forth applicable Basic I/M PSM demonstration criteria. 17 The EPA issued PSM modeling guidance establishing a means by which states conduct the required PSM demonstration, which must then be submitted to EPA as part of an I/M program certification SIP revision to the state's SIP. 18 19 As the District has an existing Enhanced I/M program, the area may demonstrate (through a PSM analysis) that the existing program meets the Basic I/M performance standard applicable to a Moderate ozone nonattainment area without modification. The state could submit this I/M certification SIP revision with the associated performance modeling and a written statement certifying their determination in lieu of submitting new revised regulations. 20 Consistent with the I/M Rule, areas with existing I/M programs need to conduct and submit a performance standard modeling analysis as well as make any necessary program revisions as part of their Moderate area SIP submissions to ensure that I/M programs are operating at or above the Basic I/M performance standard level for the 2015 ozone NAAQS. 17 See 40 CFR 51.352. 18 See EPA's “Performance Standard Modeling for New and Existing Vehicle Inspection and Maintenance (I/M) Programs Using the MOVES Mobile Source Emissions Model” (EPA-420-B-22-034, 2022). 19 See 40 CFR 51.372(a)(2). 20 See Section II.E of the Oct. 7, 2022 final rule (87 FR 60897, 60906) and the Apr. 13, 2022 proposal (87 FR 21842). To address this Basic I/M requirement for the District of Columbia portion of Washington, DC-MD-VA 2015 ozone nonattainment area required under the Moderate classification, the District submitted the June 7, 2024, SIP revision. Due to the area being designated nonattainment at a higher classification under the previous 1979 ozone NAAQS, as well as DC's inclusion as part of the CAA Northeast Ozone Transport Region (OTR), 21 the District has implemented an Enhanced I/M program since 1999. The June 2024 SIP submittal includes a PSM demonstration showing that the District's existing I/M program meets applicable, CAA-established performance requirements to achieve equivalent or greater emissions reductions than the EPA's model Basic I/M program. 21 The Washington, DC-MD-VA NAA was previously classified as Severe nonattainment under the now revoked 1979 1-hour ozone NAAQS. CAA section 184(b)(1)(A) provides that an area within a State in an ozone transport region and with a metropolitan statistical area population of 100,000 or more must implement an Enhanced I/M program. The District operates a centralized, test-only government-run inspection program (adopted by the DC Department of Energy and Environment (DC DOEE) and administered by the DC Department of Public Works (DCDPW), with emissions testing performed on a biennial basis for most vehicles (with commercial vehicles subject to more frequent annual testing of commercial passenger vehicles ( e.g., taxis and limousines) and biannual testing of school buses. Testing is required for model year 1968 and newer vehicles (up to 26,000 pounds gross vehicle weight rating (GVWR). New vehicles are exempted for the first four model years. A vehicle must pass inspection or be granted a waiver before it can be registered in the District. D. DC's Basic I/M Performance Standard Modeling Analysis and Results The District's June 7, 2024 SIP revision certifies that the existing DC I/M program (inclusive of the regulatory and other administrative program updates submitted with the June 2024 submittal, on which EPA is simultaneously proposing action upon) meets all applicable requirements for a Basic I/M program required for Moderate ozone nonattainment areas. title: Air Quality Implementation Plans; California; San Joaquin Valley; 2015 8-Hour Ozone Nonattainment Area Requirements; and California Consumer Products Regulations
content: ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY 40 CFR Part 52 [EPA-R09-OAR-2026-8252; FRL-13635-01-R9] Air Quality Implementation Plans; California; San Joaquin Valley; 2015 8-Hour Ozone Nonattainment Area Requirements; and California Consumer Products Regulations AGENCY: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). ACTION: Proposed rule. SUMMARY: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposes to approve State implementation plan (SIP) revisions submitted by the State of California to meet Clean Air Act (CAA or “Act”) requirements for the 2015 8-hour ozone national ambient air quality standards (NAAQS or “standards”) in the San Joaquin Valley ozone nonattainment area (“San Joaquin Valley” or “SJV”). In this document, the EPA refers to these submissions collectively as the “SJV 70 ppb Ozone SIP.” The EPA proposes to approve the SJV 70 parts per billion (ppb) Ozone SIP as meeting the applicable ozone nonattainment area requirements for emissions inventories, reasonably available control measures, attainment demonstration, rate of progress and reasonable further progress, motor vehicle emissions budgets, and enhanced monitoring. The EPA is also initiating the adequacy process for the budgets included in this SIP submission through this proposed rule. The EPA also proposes to approve two SIP revisions amending the SIP to incorporate changes reflecting updates to California Air Resources Board (CARB) Consumer Products Regulations and Method 310, which apply statewide and upon which the SJV 70 ppb Ozone SIP relies. These regulations concern emissions of volatile organic compounds (VOC) from antiperspirants, deodorants, consumer products, and aerosol coating products, and Method 310 is used to determine the VOC and reactive organic compounds content of these products. The EPA proposes to approve these regulations for purposes of the State's SIP under the CAA. DATES: Comments must be received on or before December 7, 2026. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews I. Overview of Proposed Action A. What action is the EPA taking? The EPA is proposing to approve certain submitted revisions to the San Joaquin Valley portion of the California SIP for the 2015 ozone NAAQS. We refer to these revisions as the SJV 70 ppb Ozone SIP, and they address the “Extreme” ozone nonattainment area requirements for emissions inventories, reasonably available control measures (RACM), attainment demonstration (including aggregate emission reduction commitments and CAA section 182(e)(5) new technology provisions), rate of progress (ROP) and reasonable further progress (RFP), motor vehicle emissions budgets (“budgets”), and enhanced monitoring. In addition, the EPA is initiating the adequacy review process for the budgets for VOC and NO X for the 2026, 2029, 2032, and 2035 RFP milestone years and the 2037 attainment year included in the SJV 70 ppb Ozone SIP. For the attainment demonstration, the EPA proposes to approve CARB's aggregate emission reduction commitments for 2037 and CARB's commitment to submit contingency measures by January 1, 2034, to cover any anticipated shortfall in emission reductions to be achieved by the plan's CAA section 182(e)(5) new technology provisions. If the EPA finalizes this proposed action, CARB's aggregate emission reduction commitments and CAA section 182(e)(5) contingency measure commitments would become federally enforceable and transportation conformity demonstrations in the San Joaquin Valley would be required to conform to the regional (whole nonattainment area) motor vehicle emissions budgets for VOC and NO X for the 2026, 2029, 2032, and 2035 RFP milestone years and the 2037 attainment year. The EPA is also proposing to approve amendments to the SIP to incorporate changes to California's consumer products regulations and CARB Method 310, which apply statewide. Specifically, the 2021 amendments to CARB's Consumer Products Regulations concern VOC emissions from antiperspirants, deodorants, consumer products, and aerosol coating products, and the 2022 amendments to CARB Method 310 are used to determine the VOC and reactive organic compounds content of these products. If the EPA finalizes this proposed action, the amended Consumer Products Regulations and amended Method 310 would be federally enforceable within the State of California. We will accept comments from the public for 30 days following publication of this proposal in the Federal Register and will consider relevant comments before taking final action. B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements? The EPA has legal authority to approve, disapprove, or conditionally approve, in whole or in part, submissions of SIPs and SIP revisions under CAA section 110(k). The applicable requirements for the actions proposed by the EPA in this document include those for SIP submissions in general, ozone nonattainment areas, motor vehicle emissions budgets, and enforceable emission limitations. For SIP submissions in general, CAA sections 110(a)(1) and (2) and 40 CFR 51.102 establish certain procedural requirements with respect to States for adoption and submittal of SIPs and SIP revisions to the EPA to meet CAA requirements. CAA section 110(l) prohibits the EPA from approving SIP revisions that would interfere with any applicable requirements concerning attainment and RFP or any other applicable requirement of the Act. For SIP submissions addressing ozone nonattainment SIP requirements, the statutory requirements are set forth in CAA sections 171 through 179B of subpart 1 (“Nonattainment Areas in General”) and CAA sections 181 through 185 of subpart 2 (“Additional Provisions for Ozone Nonattainment Areas”) and the regulatory requirements for the 2015 ozone NAAQS are codified in 40 CFR part 51, subpart CC (“Provisions for Implementation of the 2015 Ozone [NAAQS]”). In this document, we refer to these regulatory requirements and related preamble collectively as the 2015 ozone NAAQS SIP Requirements Rule (“2015 Ozone SRR”). 1 For budgets, the regulatory requirements are codified in 40 CFR 93.118(e) (“Motor vehicle emissions budgets in submitted control strategy State implementation plan revisions and submitted maintenance plans”). More specifically, the budget adequacy criteria are codified in 40 CFR 93.118(e)(4). For more detail on these requirements, as well as background on the EPA's review of the SJV 70 ppb Ozone SIP, see the applicable subsections of section II of this document for emissions inventories, RACM, attainment demonstration, ROP and RFP, motor vehicle emissions budgets, and other requirements. 1 83 FR 62998 (Dec. 6, 2018). For SIP submissions related to consumer products and aerosol coatings regulations, the applicable requirements are found in CAA sections 110(a)(2) (“Each such plan shall (A) include enforceable emission limitations . . . (E) provide necessary assurances that the State . . . will have adequate personnel, resources and authority . . .”) and 110(l). In addition, 40 CFR part 51, subpart K (“Source Surveillance”) requires SIPs to have enforceable procedures for monitoring the status of compliance with the requirements in the control strategy. For more detail on these requirements, as well as background on the EPA's review of CARB's Consumer Products Regulations, see section III of this document. II. EPA Review of the SJV 70 ppb Ozone SIP A. Background 1. Ozone Standards, Area Designations, and SIPs Ground-level ozone pollution is formed from the reaction of VOC and oxides of nitrogen (NO X ) in the presence of sunlight. 2 These pollutants, referred to as ozone precursors, are emitted by many types of sources, including on- and off-road motor vehicles and engines, power plants and industrial facilities, and area sources such as residential fuel combustion and farming operations. 2 The State of California refers to reactive organic gases (ROG) in some of its ozone-related SIP submissions. As a practical matter, ROG and VOC refer to the same set of chemical constituents, and for the sake of simplicity, we refer to this set of gases as VOC in this proposed rule. Under CAA sections 108 and 109, the EPA promulgates air quality criteria and NAAQS for pervasive air pollutants meeting certain requirements, such as ozone, to protect public health and welfare. Under CAA section 110, following promulgation of a new or revised NAAQS, States are required to adopt and submit plans that provide for implementation, maintenance, and enforcement of the NAAQS (referred to as State Implementation Plans or SIPs). Under CAA section 107(d), the EPA is required to designate areas throughout the nation as either attaining or not attaining the NAAQS, or as unclassifiable. States with designated nonattainment areas are required to submit SIP revisions to, among other things, provide for attainment within the applicable statutory timeline. In 1979, the EPA established primary and secondary NAAQS for ozone at 0.12 parts per million (ppm) averaged over a 1-hour period (“1979 ozone NAAQS”). 3 In 1997, the EPA revised the primary and secondary standards for ozone in the ambient air to 0.08 ppm averaged over an 8-hour period (“1997 ozone NAAQS”). 4 3 44 FR 8202 (Feb. 8, 1979). 4 62 FR 38856 (July 18, 1997). In 2008, the EPA lowered the 8-hour ozone NAAQS to 0.075 ppm (“2008 ozone NAAQS”). 5 Then in 2015, the EPA further lowered the 8-hour ozone NAAQS to 0.070 ppm (“2015 ozone NAAQS”). 6 On December 31, 2020, the EPA finalized its most recent periodic review of the ozone NAAQS, retaining the form and level of the standards. 7 The EPA has revoked both the 1979 ozone NAAQS and the 1997 ozone NAAQS but not the 2008 ozone NAAQS. 8 5 73 FR 16436 (Mar. 27, 2008). 6 80 FR 65292 (Oct. 26, 2015); 40 CFR 50.19. In terms of parts per billion (ppb), the level of the 2015 ozone NAAQS is 70 ppb. 7 85 FR 87256 (Dec. 31, 2020). The SIP revision that is the subject of this document relates to the requirements for the 2015 ozone standards. 8 40 CFR 50.9(b) and 40 CFR 50.10(c). In 2018, the EPA designated San Joaquin Valley as nonattainment for the 2015 ozone NAAQS and classified the area as Extreme. 9 The attainment date for areas classified as Extreme for the 2015 ozone NAAQS is as expeditiously as practicable but not later than 20 years from the effective date of the nonattainment designation. 10 Designations of nonattainment for a given NAAQS trigger requirements under the CAA to prepare and submit SIP revisions. The State of California submitted the SIP revisions that comprise the SJV 70 ppb Ozone SIP and that are the subject of this document to address the Extreme nonattainment area requirements that apply to the San Joaquin Valley for the 2015 ozone NAAQS. 9 83 FR 25776, 25790 (June 4, 2018), effective Aug. 3, 2018. 10 CAA section 181(a)(1); 40 CFR 51.1302 and 51.1303(a). Under California law, CARB is the State agency that is responsible for the adoption and submission to the EPA of California SIP revisions, and it has state-law authority to establish emissions standards and other requirements for mobile sources and certain area sources, such as consumer products. Local and regional air pollution control districts in California are responsible for the regulation of stationary sources and are generally responsible for the development of regional air quality management plans (“plans”). In the San Joaquin Valley, the San Joaquin Valley Unified Air Pollution Control District (SJVUAPCD or “District”) develops and adopts plans to address CAA planning requirements applicable to that area. Such plans are then submitted to CARB for adoption and submission to the EPA as revisions to the California SIP. Under CAA section 110(k), the EPA is charged with evaluation of each SIP revision submitted by States for compliance with applicable CAA requirements and with taking action on each submission. The EPA evaluates SIP submissions and takes action to approve or disapprove them through notice-and-comment rulemaking, including proposed and final rules published in the Federal Register . Where appropriate, the EPA may act on separate portions of a SIP submission in separate rulemaking actions. 2. The San Joaquin Valley Ozone Nonattainment Area The San Joaquin Valley nonattainment area for the 2015 ozone standards consists of San Joaquin, Stanislaus, Merced, Madera, Fresno, Tulare, and Kings counties and the western portion of Kern County. The San Joaquin Valley nonattainment area stretches over 250 miles from north to south, averages a width of 80 miles, and encompasses over 23,000 square miles. It is partially enclosed by the Coast Mountain range to the west, the Tehachapi Mountains to the south, and the Sierra Nevada range to the east. 11 The population of the San Joaquin Valley in 2020 was estimated to be more than 4.4 million people and is projected to increase to nearly 5 million people by 2035. 12 11 For a precise definition of the boundaries of the San Joaquin Valley nonattainment area for the 2015 ozone NAAQS, see 40 CFR 81.305. 12 The population estimates and projections include all of Kern County, not just the portion of Kern County within the San Joaquin Valley air basin. Summary of the State's Submissions for the 2015 Ozone NAAQS in San Joaquin Valley In this document, the EPA proposes action on all or portions of three SIP submissions, which we describe in the following paragraphs. Collectively, we refer to the relevant portions of the three SIP submissions as the SJV 70 ppb Ozone SIP. 1. SJV 2022 Ozone Plan On February 23, 2023, CARB submitted the “2022 Plan for the 2015 8-Hour Ozone Standard” (“SJV 2022 Ozone Plan”) to the EPA as a revision to the California SIP. 13 The SIP revision includes the SJV 2022 Ozone Plan main document and appendices and CARB's aggregate emissions reduction commitment specified in CARB's Staff Report titled “CARB Review of the San Joaquin Valley 2022 Plan for the 70 ppb 8-Hour Ozone Standard (Hearing Date: January 26, 2023)” (“2023 CARB Staff Report”). 14 13 CARB submitted the SJV 2022 Ozone Plan to the EPA electronically on February 23, 2023, as an attachment to a letter dated February 22, 2023, from Steven S. Cliff, Ph.D., Executive Officer, CARB, to Martha Guzman, Regional Administrator, EPA Region IX. 14 CARB's aggregate emission reduction commitment for San Joaquin Valley is described in section IV.B.2.d of the 2023 CARB Staff Report. In addition to the SIP revision, the February 23, 2023 SIP submission includes SJVUAPCD Resolution 22-12-13 (December 15, 2022), through which the District adopted the SJV 2022 Ozone Plan, and CARB Resolution 23-3 (January 26, 2023), through which CARB adopted the SJV 2022 Ozone Plan and its original aggregate emissions reduction commitment (including a subset from on-road mobile source measures for transportation conformity purposes) in support of the attainment demonstration in the SJV 2022 Ozone Plan. The February 23, 2023 SIP submission of the SJV 2022 Ozone Plan also included public process documentation at both the District and CARB levels. The SJV 2022 Ozone Plan addresses certain nonattainment area SIP requirements for San Joaquin Valley for the 2015 ozone NAAQS. More specifically, the SJV 2022 Ozone Plan includes, among other elements, an updated base year (2017) emissions inventory, RACM demonstration, RFP demonstration, attainment demonstration, motor vehicle emissions budgets for RFP milestone years and the attainment year, and enhanced monitoring. The appendices to the SJV 2022 Ozone Plan provide documentation for the emissions inventories, RACM demonstrations for stationary and mobile sources, and the photochemical modeling conducted in support of the attainment demonstration. The attainment demonstration in the SJV 2022 Ozone Plan relies on the 2022 State SIP Strategy and the aggregate emissions reductions commitment by CARB. We further describe the 2022 State SIP Strategy in section II.B.2 of this document. Also, since the submission of the SJV 2022 Ozone Plan, the District and CARB have replaced or updated certain elements of the plan, including the future year emissions inventories, attainment control strategy and associated commitments, the RFP demonstration, the motor vehicle emissions budgets, and the contingency measure elements, as discussed further below. 2. 2022 State SIP Strategy On February 23, 2023, CARB submitted the “2022 State Strategy for the State Implementation Plan” (“2022 State SIP Strategy”) to the EPA as a revision to the California SIP. 15 The SIP revision for the 2022 State SIP Strategy includes the main document itself plus CARB's resolution of adoption of the 2022 State SIP Strategy (CARB Resolution 22-14). Considered together, the 2022 State SIP Strategy and CARB Resolution 22-14 originally committed the State of California to pursue 19 new SIP measures or otherwise address each measure as described in the 2022 State SIP Strategy by the dates specified in an attachment to CARB Resolution 22-14. 16 The overall 2022 State SIP Strategy combines the commitment to pursue certain new SIP measures on a specified schedule with an aggregate emissions reduction commitment for individual nonattainment areas made at the time CARB adopted attainment plans for the individual areas. In the case of the San Joaquin Valley for the 2015 ozone NAAQS, CARB's original aggregate emissions reductions commitment was made through CARB Resolution 23-3 adopting the SJV 2022 Ozone Plan. 15 CARB submitted the 2022 State SIP Strategy to the EPA electronically on February 23, 2023, as an attachment to a letter dated February 22, 2023, from Steven S. Cliff, Ph.D., Executive Officer, CARB, to Martha Guzman, Regional Administrator, EPA Region IX. 16 The action dates specified in Attachment A to CARB Resolution 22-14 vary among the measures but range from 2021 through 2029. Implementation dates range from 2023 through 2031. 3. 2026 Extreme Ozone SIP Revision On September 23, 2026, CARB submitted the “2026 State Implementation Plan Revisions for the California Extreme Ozone Nonattainment Areas” (“2026 Extreme Ozone SIP Revision”) to the EPA as a revision to the California SIP. 17 CARB adopted the 2026 Extreme Ozone SIP Revision on July 23, 2026. The 2026 Extreme Ozone SIP Revision includes revisions to the future year emissions inventories, attainment demonstration and associated commitments, RFP demonstration, and motor vehicle emissions budgets in the SJV 2022 Ozone Plan. The budgets in the SJV 2022 Ozone Plan were derived from EMFAC2017 and the budgets in the 2026 Extreme Ozone SIP Revision are intended to update the EMFAC2017-derived budgets with revised budgets derived from the most recent EPA-approved motor vehicle emissions model for California, i.e., EMFAC2021, with off-model adjustment factors accounting for Congress' enactment of statutes disapproving the waivers of preemption previously issued by the EPA for certain CARB mobile source regulations 18 and adjustment factors accounting for the EPA's partial approval and partial disapproval of CARB's Heavy-Duty Vehicle Inspection and Maintenance Regulation (“HD I/M Regulation”). 19 The 2026 Extreme Ozone SIP Revision also includes revisions to the 2022 State SIP Strategy and revisions to the control strategy and RFP demonstration from the SJV 2022 Ozone Plan to reflect the updated budgets. ACTION: Final rule. SUMMARY: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is taking final action to approve a revision to the Maricopa County Air Quality Department (MCAQD or “Department”) portion of the Arizona State Implementation Plan (SIP). This revision establishes a federally enforceable program allowing for the generation of emission reduction credits (ERCs) by retrofitting or replacing existing on-road vehicles with lower emitting vehicles while meeting other Clean Air Act (CAA or “Act”) requirements. These ERCs are intended to be used as offsets for major stationary sources under the Department's Nonattainment New Source Review (NNSR) program. The EPA is approving this SIP revision because we find that it meets the applicable CAA requirements. DATES: This rule is effective December 7, 2026. The EPA is fully approving the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality's (ADEQ's) May 30, 2025, SIP revision for MCAQD Rule 205, “Emission Offsets Generated by Voluntary Mobile Source Emission Reductions,” revised on May 21, 2025 (“Rule 205” or “MCAQD Rule 205 submittal”). Specifically, the EPA is approving the MCAQD Rule 205 submittal by adding Rule 205 into the federally enforceable portion of the Maricopa County portion of the Arizona SIP. 1 Rule 205 allows for the generation of ERCs through voluntary on-road mobile source emissions reductions. ERCs generated by this rule are intended to be used to offset emissions increases of oxides of nitrogen (NO X ) and volatile organic compounds (VOC) at major stationary sources as part of the preconstruction permit process required by the CAA's NNSR program. 1 MCAQD developed an economic incentive program (EIP) support document that is included in Appendix 18 of the MCAQD Rule 205 submittal. The EPA's approval of Rule 205 is based, in part, on the Department's representations in this document of the actions it intends to take to implement Rule 205 and ensure MERCs are consistent with applicable CAA requirements. Therefore, the MCAQD's EIP support document is also being added to the non-regulatory portion of the Arizona SIP. B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements? We are taking this action under CAA section 110. Pursuant to CAA section 110(a), States are required to submit SIPs to the EPA that provide for the implementation, maintenance, and enforcement of the national ambient air quality standards (NAAQS). CAA section 110(k) requires SIPs to meet certain procedural requirements and requires the EPA to approve or disapprove SIP submissions. CAA section 110(l) requires States to provide public notice and an opportunity for public hearing of SIP revisions prior to their submittal and prohibits the EPA from approving any SIP revisions that would interfere with attainment or maintenance of a NAAQS, reasonable further progress, or other CAA applicable requirements. If a SIP submittal meets all the applicable CAA requirements, then the EPA must approve the submittal under CAA section 110(k)(3). In evaluating the MCAQD Rule 205 submittal, the EPA considered whether ERCs generated under the rule would meet the statutory and regulatory requirements for offsetting emissions reductions in CAA section 173 and 40 CFR 51.165, respectively. Emissions reductions may generally be credited for NNSR offset purposes under the CAA if they achieve actual emission reductions in the relevant nonattainment area that (1) are not otherwise required by the CAA or relied upon in any air quality-related programs under the CAA; (2) can be reliably quantified using methods that can be replicated; (3) will continue for the duration of the SIP or other program that relies upon the emission reductions; and (4) are enforceable by the EPA under the CAA. II. Background The MCAQD is the local air pollution control agency for Maricopa County, Arizona and is responsible for regulating stationary sources of air pollution within its boundaries. Portions of Maricopa County designated nonattainment for the 2008 and 2015 ozone NAAQS are classified as “Moderate” and portions of Maricopa County designated nonattainment for the 1987 particulate matter 10 micrometers or smaller in diameter (PM 10 ) NAAQS are classified as “Serious.” 2 In these nonattainment areas, the MCAQD is required to implement an NNSR permit program for preconstruction review of new or modified major stationary sources. 3 One of the requirements of the NNSR program is to provide surplus emissions reductions to offset a proposed project's projected emissions increases. 4 2 40 CFR 81.303. 3 The major source threshold for both VOC and NO X , which are precursors of ozone, is 100 tons per year (tpy) for the portions of Maricopa County designated as Moderate nonattainment for the 2008 and 2015 ozone NAAQS. The major source threshold for Serious PM 10 nonattainment areas is 70 tpy for PM 10 and precursors to PM 10 . See 40 CFR 51.165(a)(1)(iv). Modifications to existing major sources trigger NNSR review at different thresholds specified in 40 CFR 51.165(a)(1)(x). 4 40 CFR 51.165(a)(9)(ii). The required offset ratio for Moderate ozone nonattainment areas is at least 1.15 to 1. The offset ratio for Serious PM 10 nonattainment areas is at least 1 to 1. The MCAQD has stated that the quantity of surplus emissions reductions currently available for use as NNSR offsets do not appear sufficient to support current and projected economic growth. To incentivize the generation of additional offsets, the MCAQD developed Rule 205 to create a regulatory structure for the generation and use of NO X and VOC ERCs from a nontraditional category. Rule 205 can be used to generate NO X and VOC ERCs from on-road mobile sources, or mobile source ERCs (MERCs). The rule allows on-road mobile source fleet owners/operators that permanently reduce NO X or VOC emissions from their fleets, or credit “generators,” to trade those reductions with stationary sources, or “credit users,” who can then use them to offset their proposed NO X or VOC emissions increases for the purpose of meeting NNSR permit requirements. On April 16, 2026, the EPA proposed approving the MCAQD Rule 205 submittal because we determined that this SIP revision complied with all relevant CAA requirements. 5 Table 1 lists the materials we are incorporating into the Arizona SIP. The proposed action and technical support document (TSD) contain more information on the submittal and our evaluation. 5 91 FR 20394 (Apr. 16, 2026). Table 1—Materials for Inclusion Into the Arizona SIP Local agency Title Revised Submitted MCAQD Rule 205—Emission Offsets Generated by Voluntary Mobile Source Emission Reductions 05/21/25 05/30/25 MCAQD Revision to Arizona's State Implementation Plan (SIP) Addition of Rule 205 to the Maricopa County Air Pollution Control Regulations (MCAPCR), Appendix 18—Economic Incentive Program Support Document 05/21/25 05/30/25 III. Public Comments and EPA Responses The EPA provided a 30-day public comment period on our proposed action. The comment period opened on April 16, 2026, the date of publication in the Federal Register , and closed on May 18, 2026. 6 During this period, the EPA received comments from five separate commenters. All comments submitted during the public comment period can be found in the docket of this rulemaking. 7 6 91 FR 20394 (Apr. 16, 2026). 7 See Docket No. EPA-R09-OAR-2026-1684 for all comments submitted during the public comment period. Four commenters were supportive of the EPA's proposed action. 8 In addition to support for the proposed action, two of these commenters included additional recommendations for the EPA to consider. One commenter recommended that the EPA: (1) clarify that “future MCAQD revisions incorporating technology-neutral language for software/operational reductions” would be approvable if the offset integrity criteria are satisfied and (2) commit to updating EPA's Economic Incentive Program (EIP) guidance to clarify that “software-driven mobile source reductions can qualify for MERCs/NNSR offsets when properly documented and enforced.” Another commenter encouraged the EPA to continue to take actions that will encourage the generation of ERCs, improve the efficiency of the ERC certification process, and focus on practical actions that could meaningfully improve public health and reduce air pollution. These recommendations from commenters are outside the scope of our final action on the Department's submittal. 8 One of the supportive commenters also sent an email, with an attachment, during the comment period that was supportive of the proposed action. The email and attachment are included in the docket for this action. One commenter opposed the EPA's proposed action and requested that the EPA disapprove Rule 205. Below, we summarize the commenter's concerns and provide a response to each. Comment 1: The commenter asserted that the CAA “does not authorize stationary sources to trade credits with mobile sources because such reductions are not `permanent, quantifiable, and enforceable' as [CAA section] 173(c)(1) requires.” Additionally, the commenter stated Congress separated the authority to regulate stationary sources and mobile sources with no references to linking together with respect to generating offsets. Response 1: The EPA disagrees with the commenter's claim that mobile source emissions reductions cannot be used as offsets for stationary sources under CAA section 173(c)(1). CAA section 173(a) conditions the issuance of an NNSR permit on a determination by the permitting agency that, among other things, sufficient offsetting emissions reductions will be obtained before the new or modified source commences operation so as to represent “reasonable further progress” toward attainment of the NAAQS. 9 The required offsetting emissions reductions must be in effect and enforceable by the time the new or modified source commences operations and must assure that the total tonnage of increased emissions of the relevant air pollutant from the source is offset by an equal or greater reduction, as applicable, in the actual emissions of that air pollutant in the area. 10 Under CAA section 173(c)(1), ERCs must be obtained from the same source or other sources in the same nonattainment area, except that the reductions may be obtained from another nonattainment area if two conditions are met: (1) the other area has an equal or higher nonattainment classification than the area where the source is located, and (2) emissions from such other area contribute to a violation of the NAAQS in the nonattainment area where the source is located. 11 These restrictions are designed to ensure that offsets result in the improvement of air quality in the nonattainment area, such that construction (or modification) of the source is consistent with reasonable further progress toward attainment. 12 9 CAA section 173(a)(1). 10 CAA section 173(c)(1). 11 Id. 12 See CAA sections 173(a)(1)(A) and 173(c); see also NRDC v. EPA, 571 F.3d 1245,1267 (D.C. Cir. 2009) (noting “CAA section 173's mandate that total reductions `represent . . . reasonable further progress' ”). Consistent with these statutory requirements, the EPA's NNSR implementing regulations require that all emissions reductions claimed as offset credit be “federally enforceable” and that offsetting emissions reductions be obtained from the same source or other sources in the same nonattainment area, except that the reductions may be obtained from another nonattainment area if the two conditions specified in CAA section 173(c)(1) are met. 13 Additionally, the EPA's NNSR regulations provide that emissions reductions achieved by shutting down an existing emission unit or curtailing production or operating hours may be credited for offsets only if, among other things, the reductions are surplus, permanent, quantifiable, and federally enforceable. 14 The EPA has referred to these four creditability criteria in longstanding guidance as “integrity elements”— i.e., elements of a program that ensure it has integrity and meets applicable statutory requirements. 15 The EPA sometimes refers to these integrity elements, along with the requirement in CAA section 173(c)(1) that offsets be based on the reduction of “actual” emissions of the relevant pollutant, as the offset “integrity criteria.” 16 13 40 CFR 51.165(a)(3)(ii)(E) (requiring that all emission reductions claimed as offset credit be federally enforceable) and (F) (requiring States to follow procedures relating to the permissible location of offsetting emissions at least as stringent as those set out in 40 CFR part 51, Appendix S, section IV.D). 14 40 CFR 51.165(a)(3)(ii)(C); 40 CFR part 51, Appendix S, paragraph IV.C.3. 15 See Improving Air Quality with Economic Incentive Programs, EPA-452/R-01-001 (EPA Office of Air and Radiation, 2001) (“EIP Guidance”), available at https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2015-07/documents/eipfin.pdf ), chapter 4 (describing “fundamental principles” of all emission reduction banking and trading programs). The EIP Guidance supersedes the EPA's 1986 emission trading policy statement at 51 FR 43813 (Dec. 4, 1986). 16 See, e.g., 91 FR 20394, 20396 (Apr. 16, 2026). To the extent the commenter intended to assert that stationary sources are regulated under title I of the CAA while mobile sources are regulated under title II of the CAA, this is generally correct. But nothing in CAA section 173 or any other provision of the CAA prohibits the use of emissions reductions from mobile sources within the relevant nonattainment area for NNSR offset purposes, provided the applicable statutory and regulatory requirements are met. The commenter fails to identify any such prohibition in the text of the CAA or the EPA's implementing regulations. The commenter also fails to support its claim that mobile source emissions reductions would not meet the permanent, quantifiable, and federally enforceable offset integrity criteria. 17 The EPA's proposed rule and TSD explained in detail how Rule 205 meets the applicable CAA requirements and addresses the EPA's longstanding integrity criteria for offsetting emissions reductions. In the next few paragraphs, we briefly summarize our prior analysis of the permanent, quantifiable, and federally enforceable criteria. 17 The commenter did not raise the surplus criterion in the offset integrity criteria in this comment. To ensure emissions reductions from mobile sources meet the permanent criterion, generators of MERCs must demonstrate that replaced vehicles no longer operate in the nonattainment area (NAA) and/or that emissions do not shift to higher emitting vehicles within the fleet. Generators of MERCs do so through enforceable requirements, including robust monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements. Rule 205 contains several enforceable conditions to ensure that emissions reductions are permanent, including: limiting the applicability of the rule to “captive fleet” 18 vehicles; requiring the original baseline vehicle to be permanently removed from the Maricopa NAA or rendered permanently disabled and disposed of; 19 requiring any future replacement of the new or retrofitted fleet vehicle to be with a vehicle that is certified to the same or lower emission standard; 20 and related monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements. 21 22 18 Rule 205, section 203 defines captive fleet as, “[A] fleet of vehicles where all the vehicles in the fleet are identifiable, the locations where they are being operated can be tracked and recorded using a fleet management system, such as a global positioning system (GPS), their base of operation is in a nonattainment area, and which can serve as a permanent source of emission reductions when a vehicle is replaced or retrofitted. The captive fleet can only include on-road vehicles.” 19 Rule 205, section 302.2c. 20 Rule 205, section 302.2d. 21 See, for example: Rule 205, sections 302.2, 401.2, 401.3, 501, 503, 504, and 505. 22 For a fuller discussion on each of these requirements and how they fulfill the permanent criterion, please see pages 16 through 22 of the TSD for this action. To ensure emissions reductions from mobile sources meet the quantifiable criterion, generators of MERCs calculate emissions reductions using specific methodologies that are clear and replicable. Appendix A of Rule 205 articulates the calculation formula that MERC generators will use to determine the number of eligible MERCs. 23 Rule 205 requires MERC generators to submit information, within their MERC application, on the methodology for quantifying emissions reductions, including emissions calculations and documentation of each original vehicle's historic vehicle miles traveled. 24 25 Rule 205 also requires MERC generators to demonstrate that the captive fleet of vehicles used to generate MERCs are based and operated within the NAA. 26 Finally, Rule 205 requires the MCAQD to evaluate whether the proposed qualifying emission reductions within the application for MERCs will result in quantifiable emission reductions. 27 28 23 Additionally, section 302.1d of Rule 205 allows MERC generators to use an alternative method to quantify emissions reductions, which must go through the public participation process and receive approval from the Department and the EPA Administrator prior to use. 24 Rule 205, section 301.1a.(4). 25 See Rule 205, section 209. The original vehicle's historic vehicle miles traveled is based on original vehicle's actual vehicle miles traveled within the NAA. 26 Rule 205, section 302.1a. 27 Rule 205, section 301.2. 28 For a fuller discussion on each of these requirements and how they fulfill the quantifiable criterion, please see pages 14 through 16 of the TSD for this action. To meet the requirement in 40 CFR 51.165(a)(3)(ii)(E) that offsetting emissions reductions be federally enforceable, emissions reductions must be enforceable by the EPA and must be legally and practicably enforceable. The term “federally enforceable” is defined in the EPA's regulations at 40 CFR 51.165(a)(1)(xiv) to mean “all limitations and conditions which are enforceable by the Administrator,” including those requirements developed pursuant to 40 CFR parts 60 and 61, requirements within any applicable SIP, and any permit requirements established pursuant to 40 CFR 52.21 or under regulations approved pursuant to 40 CFR part 51, subpart I. Additionally, reductions are legally and practicably enforceable if the reductions can be independently verified; violations of the program that generated the credits are defined and those liable for the violations can be identified; access to the emissions-related information underlying the credits is available; and the public can file civil lawsuits to enforce violations. 29 The EPA's approval of Rule 205 into the SIP ensures that MERCs issued under the rule are federally enforceable. In addition, after determining that the requested reductions meet the certification criteria, the permits that MCAQD issues pursuant to its SIP-approved NNSR program incorporate requirements that make the reductions in qualifying emissions federally enforceable. 30 31 29 See EIP Guidance, pages 35 through 36. 30 Rule 205, sections 301.2 and 301.3b. 31 For a fuller discussion on each of these requirements and how they fulfill the federally enforceable criterion, please see pages 22 through 23 of the TSD for this action. Based on our evaluation, we find that Rule 205 ensures that offsetting emissions reductions will be permanent, quantifiable, and federally enforceable consistent with the requirements of CAA section 173 and 40 CFR 51.165. Comment 2: The commenter stated that Rule 205 measures emissions reductions solely at the tailpipe, relies on the EPA's MOtor Vehicle Emission Simulator (MOVES) based emission factors, and excludes “upstream NO X and VOC emissions associated with electricity generation and transmission needed to power replacement battery electric vehicles.” Therefore, the commenter believes these actions can, in effect, overstate actual emissions reductions. Because CAA section 173(c)(1) requires emissions increases to be offset by the “actual emissions” of such air pollutant within the nonattainment area, the commenter requested the EPA account for upstream “lifecycle” emissions increases associated with charging electric vehicles by “requiring MCAQD to include, at minimum, a qualitative disclosure in each MERC application identifying the electricity source and associated upstream NO X and VOC emissions.” Response 2: The EPA disagrees with the claim that to approve Rule 205 the EPA must account for upstream “lifecycle” emissions potentially associated with charging electric vehicles by requiring the MCAQD to include a qualitative disclosure in each MERC application identifying the electricity source and upstream NO X and VOC emissions. As an initial matter, we note that Rule 205 is designed to be broadly applicable, and MERCs can be generated using any fuel type ( e.g., replacing a diesel engine with a lower-emitting diesel engine). That is, Rule 205 is fuel neutral and not every MERC application will be for electric vehicles, as suggested by the comment. The commenter's concern that the use of MOVES can overstate the actual emissions reductions eligible for offsets when a vehicle is replaced with an electric vehicle raises a hypothetical, fact-specific issue that is best evaluated in the context of an individual MERC application. The commenter specifically cited to the requirement in CAA section 173(c)(1) that requires emissions increases to “be offset by an equal or greater reduction, as applicable, in the actual emissions of such air pollutant from the same or other sources in the area.” As we explained in our proposal, this means the emissions reductions must be “real” and not a theoretical reduction in the source's potential to emit; in other words, it requires that each offset represents emissions that have been taken out of the air. 32 The requirements of Rule 205 ensure that this requirement will be met. For example, before granting MERCs, Rule 205 requires the MCAQD to evaluate whether the emissions reductions will be real and include an opportunity for public comment on the Department's evaluation. 33 The rule also defines “real” as “[a] reduction in actual emissions previously released into the air resulting from a physical change or change to the method of operation by a generator.” 34 Thus, no revisions to Rule 205 are needed to ensure CAA section 173(c)(1) will be met. While the MERC calculation methodology in Appendix A of Rule 205 is meant to be applicable to most situations, if the MCAQD determines that not all of the emissions reductions for a specific project would be real, then the MERC generator could potentially obtain approval from the MCAQD and the EPA for an alternative MERC calculation method. 35 Regardless of the calculation method used, the Department must determine that the requested MERCs will result in real, quantifiable, federally enforceable, permanent, and surplus emissions reductions prior to the MERC generator requesting a permit or permit revision to impose conditions to make the emissions reductions permanent and enforceable. 36 32 91 FR 20394 (Apr. 16, 2026). 33 Rule 205, section 301.2 and 301.3a. 34 Rule 205, section 220. 35 Rule 205, section 302.1d. 36 Rule 205, section 301.2. Comment 3: The commenter stated that Appendix A of Rule 205, which contains the equation used to quantify the number of MERCs, and the MCAQD's EIP support document effectively only addresses electric vehicles. The MOVES model does not “separately represent hybrid, plug-in hybrid, CNG [compressed natural gas], LNG [liquefied natural gas], or other alternative-fuel vehicles as distinct source types” and, as a result, non-electric vehicle projects may rely on default MOVES assumptions that do not reflect actual emissions and undermine the “quantifiability and integrity of generated MERCs.” Response 3: The EPA disagrees with the commenter's claim that the quantification method in Rule 205 can only be used to generate MERCs through replacing vehicles with electric vehicles. In 2025, MCAQD revised the quantification method in Rule 205 to ensure the rule is fuel neutral. Owners/operators of vehicle fleets can opt to choose any available vehicle type as a replacement as long as it would emit less NO X and VOC, including diesel, compressed natural gas, gasoline/diesel hybrids, plug-in hybrids, and electric vehicles. The emission rates within MOVES differ by the vehicle type and by the fuel type used, as well as other aspects of vehicles and their activity. 37 38 Rule 205 identifies fuel type as one of the data points required to run MOVES. 39 Therefore, the necessary inputs to quantify MERCs are well defined in Rule 205, ensuring emissions from all fuel types are quantifiable under Rule 205. 40 41 37 MOVES categorizes vehicles into 13 source types based on physical characteristics. The source types are based on the Highway Performance Monitoring System (HPMS) vehicle groups. HPMS is defined at 23 CFR 490.101, and includes Motorcycles, Light Duty Vehicles—Short and Long Wheelbase, Buses, Single Unit Trucks, and Combination Trucks. The source types are set based on physical characteristics, such as number of wheels, number of axles, bus, truck type, etc. 38 MOVES has four tables—FuelSupply, FuelFormulation, FuelUsageFraction, and AVFT (Alternative Vehicle Fuel and Technologies)—that defines the fuels used in the area being modeled. These tables can be adjusted to accurately model the type of fuel being used at the local level. 39 See Appendix A, section A.3.(a) and Appendix A, section B.3.(a) of Rule 205. 40 See EPA's MOVES5 Technical Guidance: Using MOVES to Prepare Emission Inventories for State Implementation Plans and Transportation Conformity (EPA-420-B-24-043, Nov. 2024) for further information on how to run and implement these tools within MOVES. The EPA encourages MOVES users to contact us about the application of this guidance to specific SIPs or a regional conformity analysis. 41 As explained previously, to the extent Rule 205 does not address every possible scenario that may be encountered, generators may obtain approval from the MCAQD and the EPA for an alternative calculation methodology as prescribed in Section 302.1d of Rule 205. However, we anticipate the need for such approvals to be rare. Comment 4: The commenter stated that the surplus requirement mandates that credited reductions must not otherwise be required by the CAA and, therefore, MERCs must account for tightening Federal vehicle standards. The commenter stated that as EPA emissions standards progressively reduce NO X and non-methane organic gas emissions, “the emissions factors embedded in MOVES will increasingly reflect reductions mandated by [F]ederal law,” which would not qualify as voluntary or surplus reductions. title: Disentangling the economic opportunities of onshoring EV production in Brazil - International Council on Clean Transportation
source_name: 国际清洁交通委员会 ICCT
content: Report Disentangling the economic opportunities of onshoring EV production in Brazil Electric vehicles (EVs) are reshaping global automotive production. In 2025, one in four new cars sold worldwide were electric; in Brazil, battery electric vehicles comprised 7% of light-duty vehicle sales in the first half of 2026, more than double the market share observed in 2025. Electrification has disrupted traditional market dynamics, as many legacy automakers have struggled to keep pace with emergent EV-native manufacturers. Despite the rapid growth of EV sales, Brazil’s EV manufacturing industry remains in its infancy, with only three automakers assembling completely knocked-down (CKD) and semi knocked-down (SKD) kits domestically. Moreover, the assembly of imported EVs alone adds limited domestic content to production. Brazilian policymakers are now faced with difficult questions and trade-offs concerning how much to protect the country’s flex fuel-dominant auto industry or, conversely, to build domestic EV manufacturing capacity. The first choice risks a sizable increase in EV imports in the coming years, as further reductions in EV purchase prices are expected to drive rising sales. The second choice is promising but not easy, and entails several fundamental policy questions: How can Brazil upgrade its industrial capacities in EV manufacturing? Which parts of the value chain are worth pursuing and incentivizing? This report seeks to quantify the prospective economic benefits of producing EVs in Brazil. It estimates the economic potential of gradually onshoring EV manufacturing, battery production, and charging infrastructure investments in Brazil, and compares these estimates with recent trends in the internal combustion engine vehicle (ICEV) industry. The results focus on value added (VA)—which measures the portion of output value that is converted into national income in the form of gross domestic product—to understand which production steps hold greater economic potential and which industries stand to gain from onshoring EV production. To provide a comprehensive analysis of the EV value chain, this study uses multiregional input-output data to obtain a detailed picture of the economic potential of onshoring EV production. We increment the input-output data with a synthetic industry for EV manufacturing and a new industry for battery production while also capturing the potential of charging infrastructure investments. We assess three scenarios to model a growing extent of onshoring: the CKD Assembly scenario, in which onshoring is limited to CKD assembly; the Onshoring No Battery scenario, in which EV production is localized with no domestic battery production; and the Full Onshoring scenario, representing onshoring of the entire EV production process, including battery production. The results show that, independent of the EV transition, Brazil’s ICEV industry has experienced a decline in domestic content. The share of imported inputs used in domestic ICEV production increased from 10% in 2010 to 16% in 2022, while imported VA almost doubled in the same period, reaching 28%. This trend suggests a structural change in the country’s automotive industry in which higher VA parts and processes have been gradually offshored. In this context, we find that the gradual onshoring of EV production can capture substantial VA, even without domestic battery production. In our scenario analysis, CKD assembly alone resulted in a significant loss of domestic income compared with current ICEV manufacturing in Brazil. For every $1 spent on EVs, only about one quarter was converted into domestic VA. Upgrading Brazil’s participation in the EV value chain to produce all core EV components resulted in an 83% projected increase in domestic VA under the Onshoring No Battery scenario when compared with the CKD Assembly scenario; this scenario also achieved a VA multiplier much closer to that of current ICEV production. Finally, the Full Onshoring scenario increased domestic VA by 56% in comparison to the Onshoring No Battery scenario and achieved a VA multiplier higher than that of the ICEV industry. Figure ES1 illustrates the domestic VA generated in these three scenarios, plus a scenario with full onshoring that also accounts for the charging infrastructure investments that would be required to accommodate a moderate increase in EV adoption by 2030. Across all scenarios, substantial portions of domestic VA accrued to high-skill service industries such as legal, financial, and advertising services, as well as to wholesale and retail trade (including dealerships). In the Onshoring No Battery and Full Onshoring scenarios, manufacturing industries such as EV manufacturing, battery manufacturing, metals, and chemicals captured about half of domestic VA. We also find that Brazil is well positioned to upgrade its role in the EV value chain through the provision of industrial incentives conditioned by measurable performance criteria and limited to a pre-determined duration. Based on the modern industrial policy literature, and considering the results of the study, this analysis supports the following policy recommendations: Use existing incentives—made conditional on firm performance and with pre-established phaseout dates—to align the domestic content of Brazil’s EV production with its industrial capabilities in the near term. For example, the Brazilian government could stand firm on phasing out current SKD and, perhaps shortly after, CKD quotas by January 2027 (Moraes, 2026). This would avoid the risk associated with turning these quotas into a permanently extendable benefit, which could further delay the expansion of EV manufacturing operations beyond assembly. Adjust current policies supporting EV adoption to establish feasible and increasing local content requirements. For instance, policymakers could include domestic content requirements for light-duty vehicles as a qualifying criterion for Brazil’s new selective tax on polluting vehicles, in addition to vehicle emissions (Lei Complementar nº 214, 2025). This would help encourage consumers to purchase EVs with higher domestic content compared with imports. Create favorable conditions for battery cell manufacturing in the long term by incentivizing upstream and downstream nodes of the battery value chain. Among other measures, Brazil could extend eligibility for incentivized bond issuance (debêntures de infraestrutura and debêntures incentivadas) further downstream. The current framework already covers some battery-grade materials such as lithium carbonate and nickel sulfate (Portaria Normativa MME nº 120, 2025), but policymakers could extend the framework to more active materials such as iron phosphate and lithium iron phosphate as well as battery pack and cell assembly. On the demand side, maintaining a stable and predictable schedule of battery energy storage system capacity auctions could help attract battery-related investments alongside EV demand (Rocha, 2026).
